name: Deadlock
definition: A deadlock is a state in which every process (or thread) in a set is blocked waiting for a resource held by another process in the same set, so none of them can ever proceed without outside intervention. Deadlock can occur only if four conditions, the Coffman conditions, hold at the same time: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Ensuring that any one of the four can never hold prevents deadlock.

roles.name: Process / thread
roles.desc: An active entity that requests resources, uses them, and releases them; it blocks while a requested resource is unavailable.

roles.name: Resource
roles.desc: Something a process needs exclusive use of to continue, such as a lock, file, device, or memory buffer.

roles.name: Mutual exclusion
roles.desc: Condition 1: at least one resource can be held by only one process at a time.

roles.name: Hold and wait
roles.desc: Condition 2: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire another.

roles.name: No preemption
roles.desc: Condition 3: a resource cannot be forcibly taken from the process holding it; it is released only voluntarily.

roles.name: Circular wait
roles.desc: Condition 4: a cycle of processes exists in which each waits for a resource held by the next process in the cycle.

relations.desc: Under mutual exclusion, a resource held by one process cannot be used by any other, so a second process requesting it blocks until it is released.
Under hold and wait, a blocked process keeps every resource it already holds, so those resources stay unavailable to others while it waits.
Under no preemption, the system cannot take a resource away from its holder; only the holding process can release it.
Under circular wait, processes P1, P2, ..., Pn form a cycle in which P1 waits for a resource held by P2, P2 for one held by P3, and so on, with Pn waiting for one held by P1.
Deadlock requires all four conditions to hold simultaneously; with single-instance resources, a cycle in the resource-allocation (wait-for) graph means a deadlock exists.

Making any single condition impossible prevents deadlock: for example, acquiring resources in one fixed global order eliminates circular wait, and requesting all resources at once (all or nothing) eliminates hold and wait.

misconceptions.wrong: Deadlock is the same thing as a process waiting a really long time, or starving.
misconceptions.correct: In starvation, a process waits indefinitely while others keep making progress. In deadlock, every process in the set is blocked on another member of the set, so none of them can ever make progress.

misconceptions.wrong: A circular wait by itself is a deadlock.
misconceptions.correct: Circular wait is only one of four necessary conditions. If, for example, resources can be preempted, the cycle can be broken by taking a resource away, so deadlock requires all four conditions together.

misconceptions.wrong: To prevent deadlock, a system has to eliminate all four Coffman conditions.
misconceptions.correct: Because deadlock needs all four conditions at once, guaranteeing that any single one never holds (such as imposing a global lock order to rule out circular wait) is enough.

misconceptions.wrong: If processes are deadlocked, they will sort themselves out if we just wait long enough.
misconceptions.correct: A deadlock never resolves on its own. Recovery requires outside action such as terminating a process, preempting a resource, or rolling back; lock timeouts work only because they make a process give up resources it holds.

breaks_hint: Traffic-gridlock or two-people-in-a-hallway analogies show the circular wait but blur the other conditions, since people can back up or step aside (a form of preemption or releasing), and the shared space is not cleanly exclusive. They also make deadlock look like temporary congestion, whereas a true deadlock never clears without outside intervention.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four Coffman conditions for deadlock?
choices: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
Starvation
Circular wait
quiz.explain: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Starvation is a different liveness problem.

quiz.q: In the context of deadlock, what does the "no preemption" condition mean?
choices: A resource can be released only voluntarily by the process holding it
The CPU scheduler cannot interrupt a running process
Each resource can be used by only one process at a time
A process must request all of its resources when it starts
quiz.explain: No preemption refers to resources, not CPU scheduling: the system cannot forcibly take a held resource away. The third choice is mutual exclusion, and the fourth is a strategy for breaking hold and wait.

quiz.q: Thread T1 locks A and then tries to lock B. Thread T2 locks B and then tries to lock A. They sometimes freeze forever. Which change reliably prevents this deadlock?
choices: Give T1 a higher scheduling priority than T2
Add a short sleep before each thread's second lock call
Run the program on a machine with more CPU cores
Make both threads acquire the locks in the same order, A then B
quiz.explain: A single global lock order makes a cycle of waits impossible, eliminating circular wait. Priorities, sleeps, and more cores only change timing, so the deadlock can still happen.

quiz.q: A system requires every process to request all the resources it will need at once, and grants them all together or not at all; a process waiting for its request holds nothing. Which Coffman condition does this eliminate?
choices: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
quiz.explain: A process never holds some resources while waiting for others, so hold and wait cannot occur. Resources are still exclusive and not preempted.

quiz.q: A student says: "To make a system deadlock-free, we must eliminate all four Coffman conditions." What is correct?
choices: The student is right; all four must be removed
The student is right, except that no preemption can never be removed
The student is wrong; deadlock requires all four to hold at once, so eliminating any one of them is sufficient
The student is wrong; only circular wait matters, and the other three are irrelevant
quiz.explain: The four conditions are jointly necessary. Guaranteeing that even one of them can never hold makes deadlock impossible.

generic_lesson:
Picture two cooks sharing a small kitchen that has one knife and one cutting board. The cooks are the processes, and the knife and board are resources. Each cook needs both tools to chop vegetables. Cook 1 grabs the knife and waits for the board. Cook 2 grabs the board and waits for the knife. Neither will ever chop anything. That permanent standstill is a deadlock.

Four conditions, called the Coffman conditions, all hold here. Mutual exclusion: only one cook can use a tool at a time. Hold and wait: each cook keeps the tool they have while waiting for the other. No preemption: the kitchen rule says nobody may snatch a tool from someone else's hands; it is released only voluntarily. Circular wait: Cook 1 waits on Cook 2, who waits on Cook 1, forming a cycle.

Deadlock needs all four at once, so preventing any one of them is enough. The kitchen could require everyone to always pick up the board before the knife; with one fixed order, a cycle cannot form. It could require taking both tools together or neither. Or a manager could be allowed to take a tool back. Waiting longer does not help: a deadlock never clears without some outside action.
